beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: A slogan. Compounds how, and by how much?

beats.trigger: Run `module-7/monday.md`: test one assumption, ask for one name, talk to one person.
beats.got: Homework from a module I didn't see.

beats.trigger: **Orchestrate** three thinking disciplines against a real company question
beats.got: A learning-objectives list. Same format as every programme.

beats.trigger: The question to carry through: where is all this going?
beats.got: There is a shared folder and each person gets a subfolder. Plain enough. The closing question is the usual one.

beats.trigger: You watch one agent build another on real input. That's the whole lecture.
beats.got: A demo is coming. Fine, show me.

beats.trigger: You describe an agent; the coding agent builds it.
beats.got: I say what I want, the tool builds it. Three kinds of extension to pick from.

beats.trigger: On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand.
beats.got: Four lines: the gap, the job, inputs, one output file. I can do that, and it asks me to name a real task.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: I got a working agent file from four lines. Two years ago I'd have filed a ticket for that.

beats.trigger: "You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."
beats.got: I can test the output myself and push back on it. That's the part I believe.

beats.trigger: The room's agents form a proposal forum around it: each takes an initial stance, cross-checks with the others, publishes proposals in the shared folder, criticizes the emerging selections
beats.got: Twenty agents write documents at each other. Nine timed stages in seventy minutes. This sounds like a workshop format.

beats.trigger: Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references.
beats.got: At last, someone mentions confidentiality. In a telecom the legal team would have a view on this shared folder.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: Everyone forms an opinion before reading the others. Sensible.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: My agent reads neighbours' files and finds gaps in mine.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: An audit trail of opinions. Mildly useful.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: One agent picks, another objects, the sponsor pushes back. That is how a steering group works, only faster.

beats.trigger: From here on, every agent prompt begins by reading `midway-instructions.md` from the shared folder.
beats.got: A central instruction file steers all agents. Unclear whether that is a feature or the point where one person quietly decides.

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: Another round of critique. Nine minutes.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: The sponsor chooses what to test; the agents don't decide. Good, I expected the opposite.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: Three output files.

beats.trigger: **Risks.** Likeliest unseen pre-mortem failure; one early warning sign.
beats.got: The kernel has owners, success signals and a named risk. That is more than most strategy decks I've sat through.

beats.trigger: "You are now agent builders. You have built agents that do real work on your company's data."
beats.got: I'm told how to feel at minute seventy. This is the 'asked to be excited' moment.

beats.trigger: You do not graduate. You have a flywheel.
beats.got: Slogan again. The honest part is that the forum didn't converge first time.

beats.trigger: The room ran on its own for an hour: agents read each other's files, published, and something at the centre chose.
beats.got: A recap that sets up four observations and two questions.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The parts are the same as before; the assembly moved to the machine and specifying is the work. That I can accept.

beats.trigger: Know it before you promise a board a percentage.
beats.got: Access is not uptake. Count how many folders the kernel actually used. This is the first thing that sounds like my last three programmes.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources
beats.got: Without a citation rule agents make up what they supposedly read. A candid failure mode.

beats.trigger: A named wall means the kernel worked on something real.
beats.got: Data access, platform, discoverability. Too short to judge. Plausible.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: Skills outlast model releases. Convenient to claim, no evidence offered.

beats.trigger: Nobody in this room knows yet, and the people running this training do not know either.
beats.got: They admit half of it will be obsolete and they don't know which half. Nobody has said that to me in a training.

beats.trigger: What your company knows about its own work gets better only when somebody writes it down and somebody else picks it up.
beats.got: The model improves for free, our knowledge doesn't. True, and it sounds like every knowledge-management initiative we've run.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: Ask what evidence would make us drop the plan. I'll use this on the current steering groups.

beats.trigger: nothing in the room checked it. Hold that doubt as you did then.
beats.got: The kernel came from agents arguing with each other and no one checked it independently. They say so themselves.

beats.trigger: Kernel and agent-set files run large, so full rewrites drag.
beats.got: The agent reviews its own session and edits a file. Practical warning about slowness, which I appreciate.

beats.trigger: The agent audits itself, so the summary is not neutral.
beats.got: Don't trust the agent's own summary; ask it for a critique it ignored. Good, I can test that.

beats.trigger: Agents must cite each other's files, or they invent what they never read.
beats.got: Four bullets. The citation one is the useful one.

beats.trigger: You leave with a flywheel, not a graduation.
beats.got: The closing slogan again. The line about the useful agent being one nobody has thought of is honest, at least.

take_homes: Describing a small agent in four lines and getting a working one in minutes is real. I can run it myself and push back on it.
Access to everyone's files is not uptake; count what the output actually cites before promising anyone a percentage.
For any plan ask what evidence would make us drop it. If nobody can answer, it's a belief.

monday.move: Pick one report I assemble by hand each week, write the four-line brief, and have an agent build it. Then ask my steering group what would make us drop the current programme.
monday.when: Monday or Tuesday, if the calendar allows
monday.stop_condition: The output needs more fixing than doing it by hand, or I can't get it to cite its sources.
monday.blocker: The last programme's steering groups, and not knowing what GDPR and legal say about where the data goes.

misconception.why: Agent built from four lines was something I could check myself. 'Wait and see' still holds for the grander claims, but this part is different.

one_line: The building bit is real and I could test it. The forum and the flywheel talk was workshop theatre, but they admitted they don't know what will be obsolete, which I don't hear often.
